title: The model
lede: An {{Ontology}} is the shape, not the content: which kinds of thing may exist, what may be said about each, and what may safely be inferred. Nine modules make up this one. **None of them is approved** — they live in `ontology/draft/` and move out one at a time, by a recorded human decision.

blocks.title: In one paragraph, for a reader who does not do this for a living
blocks.text: The model is written in {{OWL 2 RL}}, a standard language for describing kinds of thing and the rules between them. The **RL** part is a deliberate restriction: it trades expressive power for the guarantee that reasoning finishes quickly and predictably. Separately, {{SHACL}} states constraints that must hold before anything is published — think of {{OWL 2 RL}} as what the model *means* and {{SHACL}} as what it *refuses to let through*.

detail.text: The addressable shapes of the corpus. Maps onto upstream's page / chunk / provision / unit, NOT onto an idealised chapter-section-paragraph tree. Chapter and Paragraph appear in the roadmap's module list and are deliberately absent here. Some Manual subsections are bold text that was never marked up as a heading, so `heading_path` is a retrieval signal and a weak structural guarantee (Q-10). The addressable unit is `chunk_ref`, and a class named Paragraph would promise a structure the corpus does not carry.

What kind of thing is speaking, and with what force. This is the module CLAUDE.md rule 5 lives in. The Manual states the Registrar's practice; it does not bind the Registrar's discretion and it is not legislation. The distinction is carried here as a class disjointness rather than as a flag, because a flag can be dropped by a projection and a disjointness cannot be satisfied by an assertion that ignores it.

The concept layer, and the module with the largest declared-but-unpopulated part of the model. Every approved concept in `eval/gold/concepts.yaml` becomes a `tmk:LegalConcept`. Whether it is also one of the four subclasses below — GroundOfRefusal, LegalTest, RelevantFactor, Exception — depends on a signed record in `eval/gold/concept-types.yaml`, and on nothing else. Deciding that 'connotation' is a LegalTest rather than a RelevantFactor is a legal judgement this repo may not make (CLAUDE.md rule 1); what it may do is hold the answer somebody gives. The owner confirmed the four groups on 2026-09-08 (OQ-0001) and the container now exists (ADR-0071). Until a concept has a type record it stays a bare `tmk:LegalConcept`, and the count of unsorted concepts is reported by every build rather than defaulted away. A machine filling these would produce a taxonomy that reads as authoritative and was authored by nobody.

ADR-0011's field list as RDF, over PROV-O. The rule this module exists to make enforceable: an assertion that cannot say where it came from does not get published. Every approved relationship in the graph appears twice — once as a direct triple so SPARQL is natural, and once as a tmk:Assertion carrying the passage, the span, the hash, the reviewer and the date. A SHACL shape fails if the first exists without the second (ADR-0058). The field list is deliberately open (ADR-0041): Stage 2 has not run, so what a machine-generated candidate needs to carry is not yet known from evidence. What is here is what the approved records actually carry today.

The closed list of predicates extraction may propose, in two halves that are never added together. **14 approved terms**, from the 35 relationships in `eval/gold/relationships.yaml` that a named expert signed. 6 of them are used exactly once, and that number is the one to read before treating this half as settled — a term seen once is a term whose boundaries nobody has tested. Every one of those 37 source refs points at `TMM/Part29`, so this half of the dictionary is what section 43 needed and nothing else. **7 authored terms**, from the 219 relationships in `authored/relationships.yaml` that a machine wrote across the whole Manual and both instruments. **No expert has read any of them.** 4 of the 7 appear in no signed record at all and exist only because the corpus outside Part 29 states relations the approved half cannot express. A predicate carries `tmk:ApprovedRelation`, `tmk:AuthoredRelation`, or both. Reading the class rather than the presence of the term is the difference between a dictionary an expert built and one a model did (ADR-0109). Domain and range are `tmk:LegalMatter` throughout. The narrow types each predicate has actually been seen with are annotations and infer nothing; see tmk:LegalMatter in the legal-concepts module for why.
Declares no classes.

Who does what, and to what. **No longer entirely unpopulated, and the change is worth stating precisely.** Until 2026-09-12 this module said that *"the approved set describes what the Manual says about section 43, not a process model of examination, and inventing one would be authoring practice"*. The first half is still true of the **approved** set and always will be — all 35 signed relationships are sourced to `TMM/Part29`. The second half described a prohibition ADR-0079 removed on 2026-09-08: authoring practice, stamped and evidenced, is the job. What now stands behind these classes is content, not a proposal. The vocabulary holds 21 concepts typed `procedural_step` and 8 typed `process_role` (ADR-0098), and `authored/relationships.yaml` holds 31 `isPerformedBy` edges joining the second to the first across the whole Manual — acceptance to the examiner, revocation of acceptance to the Registrar, opposition to the opponent. **Every one of those was written by a machine and read by nobody** (ADR-0109, ADR-0110). The role classes were declared empty to make a gap visible. Five of the nine terms the reviewer's covering note named (`review/returned/260826-expert-feedback.md`, HANDOFF Q17) now have a concept record behind them and **four still do not** — *Office Practice*, *Subject Matter Expert*, *Adverse Report* and *Team Leader* are absent from both stores. Q-28's cause is Q-53: a term's definition is usually not in a passage that cites anything, so no citation-based rule reaches them, and the boundary that was blamed for this in the first place is gone.

**Still almost unpopulated — but for a different reason than the one this comment used to give, and the difference is worth reading.** Until 2026-09-12 this module said that populating it *"is a Part 22/23 job… and Part 22 is explicitly out of the pilot scope draft"*. That sentence was true when it was written and ADR-0081 falsified it on 2026-09-08: the section 43 boundary is withdrawn, the whole Manual is in scope, and there is no part of this corpus a module may decline on scope grounds. A boundary that no longer exists was still being cited here as a live reason four days later, which is what a fence left in prose does (ADR-0110). **The real reason, measured.** 226 chunks across 37 Parts mention evidence, so the corpus has plenty to say. What the *vocabulary* holds is two concepts — `GC-0041` and `GC-0101`, both labelled *evidence of use*, and they are one of the ten duplicate-label pairs ADR-0101 put in front of the expert. Two concepts, one of them a duplicate of the other, is not a taxonomy, and declaring classes over it would produce a structure with nothing under it and an expert's name nowhere near it. So this module stays thin, and its emptiness is now a **gap with a size** — the next concept pass over Parts 22, 23, 28, 34 and the opposition Parts is what fills it — rather than a boundary. `tmk-ontology-report` counts every class here that holds nothing.

Dates, currency and what this corpus cannot answer about time. The honest headline: **point-in-time questions are out of the pilot scope draft and the snapshot cannot support them.** There is no corpus-level version stamp (Q-05); the amendment history is the upstream repository's git history, and answering 'what guidance was current on «date»' properly needs a full-history clone, which is a different data strategy rather than a different query. CQ-0014 is marked out of scope on the strength of that line. What the module does carry is the currency mechanism that actually works: staleness by content hash. An assertion whose source hash no longer matches the pin is stale and returns to review. That is Stage 10's whole incremental mechanism and it needs no version stamp.

The Stage 0 measurement artefacts, in the graph rather than beside it. This module is not in the roadmap's module list and it earns its place: it is what lets a prohibited output be a node with edges instead of a paragraph in a YAML file. PU-0004 says that attributing the Manual's 'obvious, direct and immediate' formulation to the Act is prohibited and that the error is structurally detectable. It is only structurally detectable if the prohibition, the question it attaches to, and the passages involved are all in the same graph. Here they are, and `shapes/prohibited-use.ttl` reads them.

blocks.text:
### The predicates

A {{Predicate}} is the middle of a statement — *this passage **states** that concept*. The list is **generated** from the relationships an expert approved, and a test compares the file against a regeneration. That is deliberate: a hand-written list of allowed relationships would be an agent choosing the vocabulary of the domain. To add one, have a reviewer approve a relationship that uses it.

rows.name: `ApprovedRelation`
rows.label: Approved relation
rows.search: ApprovedRelation Approved relation A predicate on the closed list in `relations.ttl` **that a named expert used in a record they signed**. Extraction may only propose relationships from the closed list. An open predicate set makes precision unmeasurable — with no fixed vocabulary, a wrong predicate and a new one are the same event, so nothing can be scored (ontology/README.md). Membership has not changed and is not expected to: the fourteen terms here come from the 35 signed relationships, every one of which is sourced to TMM/Part29. A fifteenth arrives when an expert approves a relationship that uses one.

rows.name: `AuthoredAssertion`
rows.label: Authored assertion
rows.search: AuthoredAssertion Authored assertion An assertion a machine wrote and no expert has validated (ADR-0079, ADR-0080). Deliberately NOT a subclass of tmk:ApprovedAssertion and deliberately not in the approved named graph. It is the same shape as one — same subject, predicate, object, passage, span and hash — and differs in exactly the fact that matters: nobody signed it. A query written against tmk:ApprovedAssertion therefore cannot pick one of these up by accident, which is the whole point of giving it its own class rather than a flag. It carries tmk:reviewStatus "unreviewed" and never "approved": approval moves a record to eval/gold/ through tmk-transcribe, and a record that has moved is rebuilt as a tmk:ApprovedAssertion on the next build (ADR-0086).

rows.name: `AuthoredRelation`
rows.label: Authored relation
rows.search: AuthoredRelation Authored relation A predicate on the closed list that **a machine used and no expert has read**. Added 2026-09-12 (ADR-0109). Until then the closed list was generated from the signed register alone, which was correct while an agent could not author a relationship at all — and which left the dictionary a section 43 dictionary for four days after ADR-0081 withdrew the boundary. Nothing in the fourteen approved terms can say that a concept is *defined by* a provision, that a step is *performed by* an office, or that one *must occur within* a period, and those are most of what the Manual's other 53 Parts state. A class rather than a flag, for ADR-0007's reason: a flag can be dropped by a careless projection and a class has to be asked for. A predicate both stores use carries both types, and the two usage counters beside it are never added — `tmk:usageCount` keeps its meaning as the signed count so that nothing reading it starts silently including unreviewed records (ADR-0080 consequence 3). **A term being here is not evidence the relation it names is real.** It is evidence that a deterministic pass found sentences stating it and committed to a reading, with the evidence and the doubt recorded on every record (`authored/relationships.yaml`).

rows.name: `Citation`
rows.label: Citation
rows.search: Citation Citation One reference from a passage to an authority, reified so that upstream's trust metadata survives (CLAUDE.md rule 3). A bare triple `chunk -> provision` throws away the two things that separate an author's assertion from a machine's inference, and once thrown away they cannot be recovered from the graph. So the edge is a node: it carries how it was found and how certain that was, and `tmk:citesProvision` exists beside it only as a convenience for queries that genuinely do not care.

rows.name: `LegalMatter`
rows.label: Legal matter
rows.search: LegalMatter Legal matter Anything an approved relation may hold between: a concept, a provision, a Manual passage, a decision. It exists because the approved relationships do not agree on narrower types. `requiresElement` runs Provision→Concept twice, Concept→Concept three times and Concept→Provision once; `excludesBasis` runs both ways. Asserting a narrow `rdfs:domain` on that evidence would, under OWL RL, silently reclassify every subject of the property — a careless range assertion manufactures classifications (ontology/README.md). So the asserted domain and range are this union superclass, which licenses only 'this is a legal matter', and the narrow types each predicate has actually been seen with are recorded as annotations that infer nothing. Tightening them is an expert ruling, and `tmk-ontology-report` lists the candidates.

The source graph, which is rebuilt rather than stored, populates several more (passages, citations, decisions); the ontology report counts those. An empty class is a slot waiting for content, not a bug: the four that matter most — ground of refusal, legal test, relevant factor, exception — are empty because sorting the 52 legal ideas into them is a legal judgement.
